analysis.one_liner: Raises the asset size at which banks face key consumer and trading regulations from $10 billion to $50 billion.
analysis.headline: The bill to lift federal oversight off banks with up to $50 billion in assets never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change five regulatory thresholds, each moving from $10 billion to $50 billion in assets. Banks and credit unions below the new line would escape direct Consumer Financial Protection Bureau supervision, debit-card fee limits, the ban on banks trading for their own profit, stricter mortgage underwriting rules, and would qualify for a simpler, less demanding capital test. The effect is that a much larger set of banks would be regulated like small community banks even though many are among the largest in the country.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and credit unions holding between $10 billion and $50 billion in assets — a few dozen institutions that are small only compared to the biggest banks. They would gain on five fronts at once: freedom from direct CFPB examination, the right to charge higher debit swipe fees, the ability to trade securities for their own accounts, lighter mortgage underwriting requirements, and a simpler, less stringent capital rule. Bank shareholders would capture much of this as higher profits or stock value.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the asset level for direct CFPB supervision from $10 billion to $50 billion, so banks under $50 billion would no longer face the consumer bureau's own exams for compliance with consumer financial laws.
Raises the debit interchange fee cap exemption from $10 billion to $50 billion, letting banks up to that size charge merchants higher swipe fees.
Raises the Volcker Rule threshold from $10 billion to $50 billion, allowing banks below that size to make proprietary trades and hold stakes in private funds again.
Raises the threshold for lighter ability-to-repay mortgage standards from $10 billion to $50 billion, so more banks could use less prescriptive rules when making residential mortgages.
Raises the community bank cutoff from $10 billion to $50 billion, so banks up to that size could use the simplified leverage ratio instead of the fuller risk-based capital framework.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and merchants. Bank customers at institutions between $10 billion and $50 billion would lose the direct federal examination of how those banks handle consumer complaints and product design. Merchants and the shoppers they pass costs to would bear higher debit swipe fees. Looser mortgage underwriting and lighter capital rules at mid-sized banks would add risk that taxpayers partially stand behind, since deposits are federally insured.

drawbacks.text: Consumers banking at institutions between $10 billion and $50 billion would lose the direct CFPB supervisory presence that now checks those banks' handling of complaints, fees, and product practices.
Letting banks up to $50 billion escape the debit fee cap would raise swipe fees for merchants, costs that typically show up in prices for shoppers.

Reallowing proprietary trading at banks with insured deposits, and loosening mortgage ability-to-repay standards, would rebuild some of the risk-taking and lending practices that contributed to the 2008 crisis.

The blunt 10-to-50 change does not distinguish between a genuinely local community bank and a $40 billion institution with nationwide reach, so banks far larger than the rule was designed for would get community-bank treatment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument for tailoring regulation to bank size: compliance costs weigh more heavily on smaller institutions, and a one-size rule can push smaller banks out of products entirely. But this bill does not calibrate anything — it simply quintuples every threshold at once, moving a set of very large, federally insured banks into the lighter rulebook. The savings to the banks come largely out of consumer protections that exist for identifiable reasons: direct supervision caught fee and servicing abuses, the debit cap limits swipe fees, and the Volcker Rule and mortgage standards address risks with public costs. The bill's benefits are concentrated and its risks are diffuse, and the bill offers no offsetting consumer safeguard.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Barr introduced the Financial Institution Regulatory Tailoring Enhancement Act on November 14, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.

The bill would raise five regulatory asset thresholds — CFPB supervision, debit interchange fee limits, the Volcker Rule, mortgage ability-to-repay requirements, and the community bank leverage ratio — from $10 billion to $50 billion.
The bill attracted one cosponsor in the House, a Republican.
The House Financial Services Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the full House and Senate never considered it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary bank customers and merchants are better off: direct CFPB oversight of banks up to $50 billion, debit swipe fee caps, and the proprietary-trading ban all remain in place as they were.

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.role: House Financial Services Committee member; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 14, 2023 to raise five regulatory asset thresholds from $10 billion to $50 billion.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Patrick McHenry, R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; it remained at referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no Democrat signed on, but it never reached a floor vote, so no roll call shows where each party stood.

industries.industry: Mid-sized banks and credit unions ($10B-$50B in assets)
industries.note: The bill hands these institutions five deregulatory gains at once — freedom from direct CFPB exams, higher debit swipe fees, a revived ability to trade for their own accounts, lighter mortgage underwriting, and a simpler capital rule. Each gain comes out of a protection that exists for bank customers or taxpayers.

industries.industry: Merchants and retailers that accept debit cards
industries.note: Raising the interchange-fee cap exemption to $50 billion would let more card issuers charge merchants higher swipe fees, which merchants typically pass on to shoppers in prices.

industries.industry: Large banks (over $50B) and small community banks (under $10B)
industries.note: Both ends of the size spectrum are untouched: the biggest banks keep all current rules and the smallest keep existing relief. The bill's main effect is relative — mid-sized banks would gain ground against both.
